newsitem.title: HONG KONG: No favouritism after July 1, HK regulator vows.
newsitem.headline: No favouritism after July 1, HK regulator vows.

text.p: All listed companies in Hong Kong will receive the same treatment after the territory reverts to Chinese rule on July 1, the stock market regulator said on Friday.

"They will be regulated to the full, according to Hong Kong rules. And it matters not whether it's a red chip company, blue chip company or a black chip company or whatever. Everybody will get the same treatment from us," Securities and Futures Commission (SFC) chairman Anthony Neoh said.
In a series of briefings by regulators in the last days of British rule, Neoh said there would be no changes in SFC policy.
From July 1, Hong Kong will be a Special Administrative Region (SAR) of China under a "one country, two systems" arrangement that will allow the territory a large degree of autonomy.
The Hong Kong share market has surged ahead of the event, partly on China-related stocks with a rise in volatility, but Neoh said meddling in the market was not his job.
"It's not my function to dampen sentiment," Neoh said. "It's not my function to dampen volatility. It's not my function to interfere in the market."
The SFC's job was to ensure a fair and informed market, he said.
"(If) people want to take a punt, they can jolly well do it -- provided they do it with their eyes open," Neoh said, adding that recent market volatility in some shares was up to investors.
"If the market wishes to run itself on sentiment, it will do so. I cannot influence the course of the market even if I wanted to," he said.
Neoh defended a recently announced policy on red chips -- Hong Kong-based companies with financial backing from China -- by China's State Council, or cabinet.
Red chips have surged on expectations their mainland parents will inject valuable assets into the companies.
But the State Council said asset transfers abroad into listed vehicles and Chinese-controlled company share offers abroad would need official approval.
"Clearly, the State Council has the right to regulate that," Neoh said.

Neoh said the SFC was planning for three contingencies in the local market in the short term -- a continuation of current "exuberance and higher volatility", a correction, or a "middling" market with very little volatility.
As a precaution over the handover, the SFC has imposed a tougher regime in risk management, returning to normal when markets reopen on July 3, Neoh said.
